title: The Antikythera Mechanism: Ancient Analog Computer Revealed
description: Dive into the astonishing story of the Antikythera mechanism—how a sunken bronze device from the 2nd century BC became the world’s first analog computer, what it could predict, and why its complexity vanished for 1,500 years.

sections.heading: Cold Open – The Teaser
key_points: A corroded lump of bronze from a 1901 shipwreck turned out to be a 2nd‑century BC astronomical computer.
sections.narration: What if a rusted lump from a sunken ship was actually an ancient computer? In this video we’ll reveal why that crazy idea is true and how a 2nd‑century BC Greek device could predict eclipses and the movements of the heavens decades in advance. You’ll see the shocking discovery that the Antikythera mechanism isn’t a mysterious relic but the world’s oldest analogue computer, built with dozens of interlocking bronze gears that mimic the motions of the Moon and Sun. Picture pulling a green‑tinged chunk of bronze and wood from the deep, opening it like a forgotten pocket watch, and finding a complex celestial clock that models the Moon’s speeding perigee – a trick first described by Hipparchus. Stay with us and we’ll walk through the X‑ray scans that exposed 35 meshing gears, the wooden case that protected them, and the inscriptions that unlock ancient Olympic cycles. By the end you’ll understand how this single artifact rewrote our view of ancient technology and why it still amazes scientists today.
claims: The Antikythera mechanism is an ancient Greek hand‑powered orrery built in the 2nd century BC.
It was discovered in 1901 among wreckage off the Greek island Antikythera.
It is the oldest known example of an analogue computer.
The device could predict astronomical positions and eclipses decades in advance.
It was housed in a wooden‑framed case about 34 cm × 18 cm × 9 cm in size.
Four of the recovered fragments contain gears, and inscriptions appear on many others.
The mechanism had 35 meshing bronze gears, with 30 still visible today.
It could model the irregular orbit of the Moon, where the Moon’s speed varies between perigee and apogee.
The Moon‑orbit modeling reflects studies by the astronomer Hipparchus of Rhodes in the 2nd century BC.

sections.heading: Discovery – From Wreck to Museum
key_points: Captain Dimitrios Kontos and sponge divers recovered the wreck off Antikythera at 45 m depth in 1900‑01.
Valerios Stais spotted a gear in the corroded piece on 17 May 1902, prompting the first study.
The artifact was broken into three main pieces, later catalogued as 82 fragments, four of which contain gears.
It now resides in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens, alongside reconstructions.
sections.narration: Ever wonder how a rusted lump from the sea became a star exhibit? In early 1900, Captain Dimitrios Kontos and his sponge‑diver crew from Symi hauled up a Roman cargo wreck at 45 m depth off Antikythera. They pulled up statues, glass, coins—and a mysterious bronze‑wood block. You can picture the divers hauling a 34 cm by 18 cm case, its bronze turned green by seawater. The treasure trove was shipped straight to Athens’ National Archaeological Museum. Two years passed while curators polished marble and polished bronze. Then, on 17 May 1902, archaeologist Valerios Stais, with his cousin politician Spyridon Stais, spotted a gear wheel embedded in the corroded piece. He thought it might be an astronomical clock. That single gear sparked the first study of the object. The mechanism eventually split into three major chunks, later catalogued as 82 fragments. Four of those fragments still hold gears, the largest about 13 cm across with 223 teeth. All pieces now sit in the museum alongside detailed reconstructions. Curious how those fragments were reassembled? We’ll see how scholars teased the bronze brain apart in the next reveal.

sections.heading: Design & Mechanics – Inside the Bronze Brain
key_points: The device housed 35 meshing bronze gears; 30 are still visible in the fragments.
The largest gear measured about 13 cm (5 in) diameter with 223 teeth.
It modeled Sun and Moon motion, eclipse prediction, and the irregular lunar orbit using epicyclic gearing.
A hand crank linked to a crown gear moved all interlocked gears, driving multiple dials simultaneously.
sections.narration: Inside the bronze case, thirty‑five bronze gears interlock like a tiny machine city. Thirty of those gears still peek out from the surviving fragments. The biggest wheel spans about 13 cm, its rim crowded with 223 teeth. Imagine you turning that hand crank and feeling the whole constellation shift. The crank connects to a crown gear that drives the largest wheel. One turn spins the date pointer and nudges every other gear at once. This cascade powers dials that trace the Sun’s path across the zodiac. You can picture the Moon’s wobble captured by epicyclic gears inside. Those epicyclic teeth accelerate the Moon when it nears perigee and slow it near apogee. How could such precise astronomy fit in a hand‑held box? The answer lies in the clever gear ratios, each tooth count tuned to celestial cycles. So when you twist the crank, the mechanism simultaneously predicts eclipses, lunar phases, and solar positions. Every gear teeth meshes perfectly, turning the bronze brain into an ancient analog computer. Stay tuned, because the next reveal shows how scientists peeled back the rust to read its secrets.

sections.heading: Functions – Calendars, Eclipses, and Games
key_points: Front dial: fixed zodiac ring plus a movable Egyptian calendar ring (12 months, 30 days + 5 intercalary days).
Rear dials tracked the 19‑year Metonic cycle, the 18‑year Saros eclipse cycle, and a four‑year athletic‑games cycle similar to the Olympiad.
A lunar phase indicator used a half‑black, half‑white ball driven by a differential gear.
Inscriptions reveal numbers linked to Venus and Saturn synodic cycles, suggesting planetary calculations were also intended.
sections.narration: You’ve probably seen that weird bronze clock with two rings. The front ring stays still, marked with the twelve zodiac signs. The outer ring spins, showing the Egyptian calendar – twelve months of thirty days plus five extra days. Turn the crank and the calendar ring slides against the zodiac, lining dates with the stars. How does it handle longer cycles? On the back, three dials spin: a 19‑year Metonic cycle, an 18‑year Saros eclipse cycle, and a four‑year games cycle like the ancient Olympiad. Each full turn moves tiny pointers over engraved numbers. Ever wonder how the Moon’s face changes? A half‑black, half‑white ball on a differential gear spins, displaying the real‑time lunar phase. The mechanism even carries numbers for Venus and Saturn’s synodic periods, hinting at planetary forecasts. Picture the gears clicking, each tooth advancing a calendar, an eclipse, a game, or a planet’s return. What mystery still hides in those bronze gears? The next reveal will show how scientists stripped away rust to read the hidden planetary calculations.

sections.heading: Scientific Investigation – Uncovering the Secrets
key_points: 2005: Cardiff University team (Mike Edmunds) used X‑ray tomography to image internal gears and read faint inscriptions.
sections.narration: What did they see when they sliced through centuries of rust? In 2005 a Cardiff University team, led by Mike Edmunds, pointed an X‑ray scanner at the bronze brain. The machine buzzed, sending high‑resolution X‑rays through each fragment. Images popped up, revealing tiny teeth and faint letters hidden beneath the corroded shell. You could actually count the gears – thirty‑five meshing bronze wheels, though only thirty still show up in the scans. The biggest gear is about 13 cm across and has 223 teeth. Did you ever wonder how the ancients could model the Moon’s wobble? The scans uncovered a gear train that mimics the Moon’s irregular orbit – faster at perigee, slower at apogee – the exact pattern Hipparchus of Rhodes studied in the 2nd century BC. The X‑ray images also exposed ghostly inscriptions that once covered the outer casing. Those numbers link to the synodic cycles of Venus and Saturn, a link confirmed in 2016. So the rust wasn’t a barrier; it was a veil that the X‑ray peeled away, exposing the mechanism’s true complexity. What hidden part might still be missing, waiting for the next breakthrough?

sections.heading: Payoff – Legacy and Mystery
key_points: The mechanism predates the shipwreck (dated ~70–60 BC) and was likely calibrated around 23 Dec 178 BC or 204 BC.
Its complexity was unmatched until 14th‑century European astronomical clocks, a gap of ~1,500 years.
Scholars link its design to Hellenistic astronomers such as Hipparchus and possibly the school of Archimedes.
The Antikythera mechanism remains a testament to ancient Greek engineering, showing that analog computation existed millennia before modern computers.
sections.narration: What does a bronze brain from 200 BC mean for you? It tells you the Antikythera mechanism predates its 70‑60 BC shipwreck by decades. Some scholars calibrate it to 23 December 178 BC; others argue for 204 BC. You’re looking at gearwork that out‑classed anything for roughly 1,500 years until 14th‑century European clocks appeared. How could such complexity arise so early? The design links to Hellenistic astronomers like Hipparchus and perhaps Archimedes’ school. Picture a wooden case about 34 cm × 18 cm × 9 cm, a 13 cm gear with 223 teeth, all hand‑crafted. Does this change your idea of ancient engineering? Yes—it proves analog computation existed millennia before modern computers. The device could predict eclipses and Olympic cycles decades ahead. It was discovered in 1901 among wreckage off Antikythera and split into 82 fragments, four of which hold gears. The largest gear measured about 13 cm in diameter. Researchers in 2022 suggested the initial calibration date, not construction date, could be 23 December 178 BC; other experts favor 204 BC. Machines this complex didn’t reappear until the 14th century. Your takeaway: Hellenistic Greeks built the first known analogue computer, far ahead of the medieval clockwork age.
